The English Channel crossing from France to the UK remains a dangerous journey for people hoping to reach British shores. https://balkaninsight.com/2026/07/22/rom.text: Western city of Oradea again says no to Pride Parade for fourth consecutive year – adding to concerns about backsliding on LGBTQ+ rights in the EU-member country. Oradea’s unauthorised Pride March in 2025. Photo: Photo: Ovi D. Pop/Oradea Pride. Just over 250 kilometres separate Romania’s western city of Oradea from Budapest in Hungary, but until recently the two cities shared another distinction: both had refused to allow Pride marches. Hungary’s capital hosted a Pride event this year despite government opposition. Oradea is now the only major city in the European Union where local authorities continue to deny permission for a Pride march, after refusing to authorise the 2026 event on Wednesday. “The City Hall has decided not to approve the event. All 115 possible routes proposed by the organisers are concentrated in the city’s central area … These routes are unavailable because they overlap with other authorised events, or are affected by major public infrastructure works,” municipal spokesperson Octavian Haragoș said, as quoted by the local news outlet ebihoreanul.ro . The municipality did not explain why alternative routes outside the city centre could not be considered. The decision followed weeks of delays by the city council in ruling on the organisers’ request, where conservative councillors and religious groups dominated the debate. Human rights groups condemned the decision, arguing that it violates the constitutional right to peaceful assembly. “We consider this decision completely unacceptable because it effectively blocks people’s constitutional right to peaceful assembly,” Victor Ciobotaru, director of ACCEPT, Romania’s leading LGBTQ+ rights organisation, told BIRN. “Under Romanian law, local authorities cannot ban a public march. Their role is to identify practical solutions to ensure that such events can take place safely and under appropriate conditions, not to prevent them altogether,” Ciobotaru added. Citing the same legal argument, ARK Oradea, the organisation behind the city’s Pride Parade, said the march would go ahead on July 25 despite the municipality’s refusal to authorise it. “Our march will take place … As a sign of solidarity and concern for the situation in Oradea, representatives of nine diplomatic missions accredited to Romania, as well as representatives of the Ombudsman Institution, will be present in Oradea to monitor the unfolding of events,” ARK said, adding that the presence of diplomats reflects growing international concern over restrictions on freedom of assembly and LGBTQ+ rights in Romania. This marks the fourth consecutive year that Oradea’s authorities have refused to authorise the Pride Parade. Last year, however, an unauthorised march was still held through the city centre, attended by several hundred mostly young people. There were brief scuffles between some participants and the police but the situation did not escalate. Authorities later imposed fines totalling 19,800 lei (about 3,900 euros) on organisers and participants in the unauthorised march Romania has made progress on LGBTQ+ rights since joining the European Union in 2007 but continues to rank among the bloc’s weakest performers in terms of legal protections and social acceptance. Consensual same-sex relations have been legal since 2001, but same-sex marriage and civil partnerships are not recognised, despite a 2023 ruling by the European Court of Human Rights requiring Romania to provide legal recognition and protection for same-sex couples. Public attitudes toward LGBTQ+ people remain largely conservative, particularly outside major cities. Pride marches have been held annually in Bucharest for two decades, however, and in several other cities, generally under police protection and without major incidents. Human rights organisations have urged Romania to strengthen anti-discrimination protections and fully implement European human rights standards, arguing that it is lagging behind in terms of the country’s commitments as an EU member. Photograph: RJ Hawkins/Wildlife Conservation Society Education Dept New York Otter spotted for first time in 100 years in New York City’s Bronx River Image captured in early June shows animal foraging in the waterway in first since early 1900s, signaling its recovery Oliver Milman Wed 19 Aug 2026 13.27 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An otter has been spotted in the Bronx River for the first time in more than 100 years, in a further sign that New York’s previously befouled waterways are recovering some of their ecological health. The North American river otter was photographed by a motion-activated camera foraging near some vegetation in the Bronx River, a waterway that flows through New York’s Bronx and empties into the East River. The image, captured in June by the camera of RJ Hawkins, a scientist affiliated with the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx zoo, is the first documented sighting of a river otter in the river since the early 1900s, according to the society. Netanyahu party campaign billboard likens Mamdani to leaders of Iran and Hezbollah Read more “When I first reviewed the images, I could hardly believe what I was seeing,” said Hawkins. “Knowing this may be the first documented river otter in the Bronx in generations was an incredible moment. It shows why long-term wildlife monitoring and environmental restoration efforts matter.” River otters are found across North America and were once plentiful in New York’s rivers but vanished due to rampant water pollution, habitat loss and trapping for their fur. The Bronx River, in particular, was treated as an open sewer and a dumping ground for New York’s rapidly expanding industrial base as the city grew into an economic powerhouse in the 19th and 20th centuries. Factories and slaughterhouses dumped chemicals, oil and animal blood directly into the water, with untreated sewage also seeping into the waterway. The river faced the further indignity of becoming a sort of garbage tip, as people threw old tires, appliances and other unwanted materials into it. This decimated local wildlife, but concerted conservation efforts and laws such as the Clean Water Act have in recent years helped restore the Bronx River’s fortunes, to the point that species such as oysters have returned. In 2007, beavers returned to the river for the first time in more than 200 years, the zoo said, and the appearance of a river otter suggests the waterway, which is New York City’s only freshwater river, is continuing to recover from decades of pollution. While the sighting of a single otter doesn’t confirm a larger resident population, it is encouraging as river otters require clean water and abundant fish. Measuring up to 5ft in length and sporting a muscular tail that comprises 40% of their body, river otters are considered playful creatures and adept hunters. When frightened, they can emit a scream that can be heard 1.5 miles away. “There are moments in conservation that remind us why this work matters, and this is one of them,” said Craig Piper, director of Bronx zoo. “Thanks to a broad coalition of public and private partners, we can celebrate the return of an otter as a result of decades of restoration work to provide cleaner water and healthier habitat. It’s a win for both wildlife and people.” Explore more on these topics New York Wildlife Animals Rivers news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light
